mean: to interrupt someone mid-story and spoil it
lit: to break the waist of a story: snap it in the middle so it can no longer stand up

use.how: Verb phrase with a person (or an interruption) as subject: 人の話の腰を折る. Common as an apology before cutting in: 話の腰を折って悪いけど.

near.diff: 口を挟む is simply cutting into a conversation; 話の腰を折る stresses that the interruption broke the flow of someone's story or explanation.
水を差す dampens a mood or a plan; 話の腰を折る breaks off what someone is in the middle of saying.

cue: Your friend is just reaching the funny part of her travel story when your brother asks what's for dinner, and she loses the thread.

ctx.s: 弟[おとうと]はいつも人[ひと]の{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]る}。
ctx.en: My little brother always cuts in on people's stories.

ctx.s: 「{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]って}ごめん、それっていつの話[はなし]？」
ctx.en: "Sorry to interrupt, but when was this?"

ctx.s: 面白[おもしろ]いところだったのに、電話[でんわ]が鳴[な]って{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]られた}。
ctx.en: It was just getting to the good part when the phone rang and broke off the story.

ctx.s: せっかく盛[も]り上[あ]がってきたところなのに、{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]らない}でよ。
ctx.en: It was just getting good, so don't break off my story!

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]が冗談[じょうだん]で{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]った}せいで、彼女[かのじょ]は何[なに]を言[い]おうとしていたか忘[わす]れてしまった。
ctx.en: Because he cut in with a joke, she forgot what she had been about to say.

ctx.s: 相手[あいて]の{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]らず}、最後[さいご]まで聞[き]くのが聞[き]き上手[じょうず]のこつだ。
ctx.en: The secret of being a good listener is to hear people out without breaking in.

bad.s: 資金[しきん]不足[ぶそく]で、工場[こうじょう]の建設[けんせつ]工事[こうじ]が{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]られた}。
bad.en: (meant: a lack of funds halted the factory construction)
bad.why: It is about breaking off someone's talk in mid-flow, not halting a project. For work stopped partway, say chūdan sareta or tonza shita.

bad.s: 私[わたし]は{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]って}、先生[せんせい]の説明[せつめい]を静[しず]かに聞[き]いた。
bad.en: (meant: I sat attentively and listened quietly to the teacher)
bad.why: It does not mean bowing or listening respectfully; it means interrupting, the opposite of listening quietly.

mean: to feel a chill of horror
lit: one's spine goes cold: the shiver that runs down the back at something frightening

use.how: Predicate about the speaker's reaction to something eerie or to a danger just realised: 考えただけで背筋が寒くなる. Often 背筋が寒くなるような話.

near.diff: 鳥肌が立つ can also come from cold, disgust or being deeply moved; 背筋が寒くなる is only a chill of fear or horror.
冷や汗をかく is the nervous sweat of a tight spot you are in; 背筋が寒くなる is the chill of dread, often on realising what could have happened.

ctx.en: "They say this really happened." "Stop it, you're giving me the creeps."

bad.s: 今朝[けさ]は気温[きおん]が低[ひく]くて、{背筋[せすじ]が寒[さむ]くなった}。
bad.en: (meant: it was so cold this morning that I felt chilly)
bad.why: The chill is one of fear, not of temperature. For being cold, just say samukatta.

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]の歌声[うたごえ]があまりに美[うつく]しくて、{背筋[せすじ]が寒[さむ]くなった}。
bad.en: (meant: her singing was so beautiful it gave me goosebumps)
bad.why: It is only for fear or horror. Being thrilled or moved is torihada ga tatsu.

mean: a last-ditch stand with no way to retreat
lit: a battle formation with its back to the water: no room to fall back

story.text: In the wars that founded the Han dynasty, the Han general Han Xin attacked the larger army of Zhao. Against the usual rules of warfare he drew up his troops with a river at their backs, so they could not run. Knowing there was no retreat, his soldiers fought desperately, while a hidden force seized the Zhao camp, and Han Xin won a famous victory.
story.source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (史記), biography of Han Xin (淮陰侯列伝)

use.how: A noun: 背水の陣で臨む, 背水の陣を敷く, or 背水の陣だ. Said of oneself or others committing to a do-or-die effort with no fallback.

near.diff: 腹をくくる is making up your mind to face something; 背水の陣 is the situation of having no way back, often one you set up on purpose.
正念場 is the decisive moment that tests you; 背水の陣 is the stance of fighting with every retreat cut off.

cue: A runner quits her job, sells her car and moves abroad to train full-time: if she misses this Olympics, she has nothing to go back to.

ctx.s: 今年[ことし]落[お]ちたらもう後[あと]がない。{背水[はいすい]の陣[じん]}で試験[しけん]に臨[のぞ]む。
ctx.en: If I fail this year, there's no next time. I'm going into the exam with my back to the wall.

ctx.s: 会社[かいしゃ]を辞[や]めて店[みせ]を開[ひら]いたのだから、まさに{背水[はいすい]の陣[じん]}だ。
ctx.en: He quit his company to open the shop, so it's truly do or die.

ctx.s: 「貯金[ちょきん]を全部[ぜんぶ]使[つか]うの？」「うん、{背水[はいすい]の陣[じん]}を敷[し]くつもり。」
ctx.en: "You're using all your savings?" "Yes, I'm burning my bridges."

ctx.s: 二連敗[にれんぱい]したチームは、{背水[はいすい]の陣[じん]}で第三戦[だいさんせん]を迎[むか]えた。

ctx.en: With poor results continuing, the company launched its new product as a last-ditch bid.

ctx.s: 引退[いんたい]をかけた{背水[はいすい]の陣[じん]}の試合[しあい]で、彼[かれ]は見事[みごと]に勝[か]った。
ctx.en: In a do-or-die match with his career on the line, he won brilliantly.

bad.s: 今日[きょう]は{背水[はいすい]の陣[じん]}で、川[かわ]のそばでのんびりバーベキューをした。
bad.en: (meant: today we had a relaxed barbecue by the river)
bad.why: It is not about being near water; it means a desperate stand with no retreat, which a relaxed day out is the opposite of.

bad.s: 失敗[しっぱい]してもまた来年[らいねん]受[う]ければいいので、{背水[はいすい]の陣[じん]}で気楽[きらく]に挑戦[ちょうせん]する。
bad.en: (meant: I can always retake it next year, so I'll take it easy)
bad.why: The whole point is that there is no second chance. If you can try again, it is not a last stand with your back to the river.

lit: not putting a cloth over one's teeth: words come out bare, not wrapped or softened

use.how: Before a noun about speech: 歯に衣着せぬ物言い, 歯に衣着せぬ発言. Adverbial form 歯に衣着せずに言う. Can be admiring or wary, depending on context.

near.diff: 口が悪い is a habit of rude, harsh language; 歯に衣着せぬ is frankness, saying the plain truth without softening it, and may be admired.
身も蓋もない criticises a remark so blunt it leaves nothing to say; 歯に衣着せぬ describes a person's frank way of speaking.

ctx.en: Her unvarnished remarks sometimes make the people around her nervous.

ctx.en: At the press conference the coach bluntly criticised his players' lack of preparation.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{歯[は]に衣[きぬ]着[き]せぬ}人[ひと]なので、いつも遠回[とおまわ]しに丁寧[ていねい]に話[はな]す。
bad.en: (meant: he is careful, so he always speaks politely and indirectly)
bad.why: It means the opposite: speaking frankly with nothing softened. Indirect, careful speech is tōmawashi na iikata.

bad.s: その政治家[せいじか]は{歯[は]に衣[きぬ]着[き]せぬ}嘘[うそ]を平気[へいき]でつく。
bad.en: (meant: that politician tells shameless lies without blinking)
bad.why: It praises or notes frankness, saying what one really thinks; it cannot describe lying. For shameless lies, say heiki de uso o tsuku.

mean: to put a brake on a trend
lit: to put on the brake: a wheel chock or brake that stops something from rolling on

use.how: Takes に: 人口減少に歯止めをかける. Said of curbing an unwelcome trend (decline, rising costs, excess). Intransitive form 歯止めがかかる / かからない.

near.diff: 待ったをかける halts a specific plan or action; 歯止めをかける curbs an ongoing trend such as falling sales or rising prices.
拍車をかける speeds a trend up; 歯止めをかける slows or stops it. They are opposites.

ctx.en: The government announced various measures to halt the falling birth rate.

ctx.en: With the new coach's arrival, the team's losing streak was finally halted.

ctx.s: 森林[しんりん]の減少[げんしょう]に{歯止[はど]めをかける}には、国際的[こくさいてき]な協力[きょうりょく]が欠[か]かせない。
ctx.en: International cooperation is essential to check the loss of forests.

bad.en: (meant: the light was red, so I braked my bicycle)
bad.why: As an idiom it curbs a trend, not a vehicle. To brake a bike, say burēki o kaketa.

bad.s: 好調[こうちょう]な売[う]り上[あ]げにさらに{歯止[はど]めをかけて}、もっと伸[の]ばしたい。
bad.en: (meant: we want to push our strong sales even higher)
bad.why: It stops a trend; it cannot boost one. To accelerate a trend, say hakusha o kakeru.

lit: to curl up one's tongue: so impressed that words fail you

use.how: Verb phrase, often 〜に舌を巻く or 舌を巻くほど. Said of being amazed at someone else's skill, talent or knowledge, often beyond what was expected.

near.diff: 目を見張る is being struck by anything remarkable, a sight or a change; 舌を巻く is admiration specifically for someone's ability.
頭が下がる is respect for someone's effort or attitude; 舌を巻く is amazement at their skill.

bad.en: (meant: I was dumbfounded by his rude behaviour)

mean: to feel stifled by a tense atmosphere
lit: one's breath gets blocked: as if the air in the room were too thick to breathe

use.how: Predicate about a place, a relationship or an atmosphere that feels oppressive: 息が詰まりそうだ, 息が詰まるような沈黙. Often with ような or そう.

near.diff: 息を呑む is a sudden gasp at something surprising or beautiful; 息が詰まる is the lasting, suffocating feeling of a tense or oppressive situation.
間が持たない is the awkwardness of not knowing what to say to fill time; 息が詰まる is feeling suffocated by pressure or strictness.

mean: to come back to life, to make a comeback

near.diff: 軌道に乗る is something new getting going smoothly; 息を吹き返す is something that was nearly dead coming back to life.
日の目を見る is something hidden finally becoming known; 息を吹き返す is something failing reviving.

ctx.en: With tourists returning, the run-down hot-spring town has come back to life.

bad.en: (meant: the new shop was busy from its first day)

mean: to harden one's heart for someone's own good

near.diff: 血も涙もない condemns a person as truly heartless; 心を鬼にする is a caring person acting strict on purpose, for the other's sake.

mean: to mend one's ways and start afresh
lit: to swap out one's heart: take out the bad one and put in a new one

use.how: Usually 心を入れ替えて + a new behaviour (頑張る, 真面目に働く). Said of someone giving up a bad attitude or habit, often after a scolding or failure.

near.diff: 足を洗う is quitting a bad line of work or way of life; 心を入れ替える is a change of attitude, being more serious or diligent from now on.
気を取り直す is pulling yourself together after a disappointment; 心を入れ替える is reforming after behaving badly.

cue: After failing a year for skipping classes, a student promises his parents that from now on he will attend every lecture and study properly.
